<Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.>: We oppose H.R. 4214, the ``Clean Air and Building Infrastructure Improvement Act'' which seeks to amend the Clean Air Act (CAA) to give new sources of pollution ``amnesty'' from new air quality standards, leaving existing facilities with the burden to do more to reduce their emissions if the area is near or in nonattainment--raising the cost of cleaning up pollution, and worsening air quality overall. For over half a century, the CAA has improved air quality and public health, while simultaneously giving states the flexibility needed to ensure sustained economic development and industrial growth. H.R. 4214 would undercut the critical public health protections provided by the CAA, to do the bidding of corporate polluters.
BACKGROUND
The CAA requires EPA to set National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for certain pollutants that endanger public health and the environment.\1\ These health-based standards are the cornerstone of the CAA. EPA sets primary NAAQS at concentration levels sufficient to protect the public health with an ``adequate margin of safety.'' For the six criteria pollutants--lead, particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen dioxide (NO<INF>2</INF>), sulfur dioxide (SO<INF>2</INF>), and carbon monoxide--the primary NAAQS identifies the level of ambient air pollution that is ``safe'' to breathe. While costs are not considered in establishing these standards at the federal level, costs can be and are considered by states in developing plans to meet the standards.
\1\Clean Air Act at Sec. 109.
In particular, fine particulate matter (PM <INF>2.5</INF>) poses significant health risks--especially to children, pregnant women, and underserved populations. Studies have linked PM<INF>2.5</INF> to numerous adverse health impacts, ranging from increased asthma attacks and lung disease to premature death. To address the risks of PM<INF>2.5</INF> exposure, EPA issued a final rule strengthening the primary annual PM<INF>2.5</INF> NAAQS from 12 micrograms per cubic meter ( g/m<SUP>3</SUP>) to 9  g/m<SUP>3</SUP> in 2024.\2\ This decision was based on the review of thousands of studies showing effects of PM<INF>2.5</INF> on public health and welfare and was consistent with the recommendations of the independent Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee (CASAC). The updated PM<INF>2.5</INF> NAAQS had an estimated net benefit of up to $46 billion annually in 2032 alone.\3\ However, EPA Administrator Zeldin announced that the Agency would reconsider the 2024 PM<INF>2.5</INF> NAAQS, threatening to leave Americans exposed to dangerous levels of air pollution.\4\ That said, EPA's own estimates show that by 2032--the earliest year states would need to meet the updated standard--99 percent of counties would meet the 2024 PM<INF>2.5</INF> standard.\5\
\2\Environmental Protection Agency, Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter, 89 Fed. Reg. 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024) (final rule).
\3\Environmental Protection Agency, Final Rule to Strengthen the National Air Quality Health Standard for Particulate Matter Fact Sheet (Feb. 2024) (https://www.epa.gov/system/files/ documents/2024-02/pm-naaqs-overview.pdf).
\4\Environmental Protection Agency, Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5) to Aid Manufacturing, Small Businesses (Mar. 12, 2025) (press release).
\5\Environmental Protection Agency, Final Rule to Strengthen the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (Feb. 7, 2024) (https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024 02/2024-pm-naaqs-final-overview-presentation.pdf).
The CAA also requires the owner or operator of any new or expanded source of air pollution to obtain permits before construction begins, ensuring that new and expanding facilities will not increase pollution above levels that are safe to breathe. The preconstruction permitting provisions achieve this by requiring new and modified sources to use control technology to reduce their emissions; and to assess, and if necessary, address their remaining air quality impacts. This approach ensures that both the facility and community can mitigate any increase in pollution before building begins, when it is most cost-effective.
SUMMARY OF THE CLEAN AIR AND BUILDING INFRASTRUCTURE IMPROVEMENT ACT
Section 2 amends CAA Section 109 to require EPA to concurrently publish implementing guidance with any final rule updating a NAAQS. If EPA fails to do so, new or expanding facilities would be allowed to apply for a preconstruction permit based on the old air quality standard. This arbitrary requirement would give new sources of pollution ``amnesty'' from new, and more protective air quality standards, or artificially delay the issuance of an updated NAAQS entirely. Both outcomes would harm public health and are inconsistent with the goals of the CAA.
Testimony before the Committee indicated that EPA publishing concurrent implementation guidance is unnecessary for states to do their job protecting the public from air pollution. States have a wealth of experience with the NAAQS revision process and the preconstruction permit program, which was established in the 1980s.\6\ As a practical matter, it is not always feasible or advisable for EPA to issue concurrent implementation regulations and guidance when revising a NAAQS, since most guidance develops organically as result of consultation with state and local air agencies and affected sources after they begin the process of implementing the NAAQS.
\6\House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Testimony of John D. Walke, Federal Clean Air Director, Natural Resources Defense Council, Hearing on ``Short-Circuiting Progress: How the Clean Air Act Impacts Building Necessary Infrastructure and Onshoring American Innovation'', 119th Cong. (June 11, 2025).
Section 3 includes a grandfathering provision that allows-- in certain circumstances--pending permit applications to avoid compliance with the updated 2024 PM<INF>2.5</INF> NAAQS. For areas with unhealthy air, pollution is a zero-sum game: an increase in pollution in one place must be offset by a reduction elsewhere. So, if new or expanding facilities are allowed to emit more, existing facilities will have to cut emissions to make up for that extra pollution. That is unfair and makes it more expensive to achieve healthy air.
Despite the hyperbolic claims, the history of the CAA shows that an updated PM<INF>2.5</INF> NAAQS will not end the construction of new facilities in the United States. In reality, thousands of facilities have been constructed since the inception of the preconstruction permit program nearly 50 years ago. EPA has updated numerous NAAQS based on new science and public health information, and industry has always innovated new advanced technologies to protect the public health of neighboring communities.
CONCLUSION
H.R. 4214, if enacted, would give certain facilities a free pass on CAA requirements, and expose Americans to dangerous air pollution. The bill also shifts the burden of environmental compliance to older facilities that will have to do more than their fair share to keep areas in attainment with a NAAQS. At the Full Committee Markup, Democrats offered amendments to address the problematic amnesty provision, and to ensure the bill's loopholes wouldn't benefit old coal plants operating under Section 202(c) ``must-run'' orders. All efforts to improve the bill were defeated on party-line votes.
H.R. 4214 is nothing more than dangerous clean air rollbacks and industry exemptions rebranded as ``permitting reform.'' With this bill, the majority would allow polluters to override scientists, leading to air quality standards based on industry profits rather than public health, leaving our communities exposed. For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 4214.
Frank Pallone, Jr.,
Ranking Member.
